A&P / Tissue identification

How to identify epithelial tissue.

Start with the architecture, not the memorized name. Count the layers, inspect the cells at the free surface, then use the location and job as a cross-check.

See the four patterns ↓Try the questions
STUDY BENCH / A&P 002LOOK · NAME · CHECK

One reliable sequence.

Layers → cell shape → special features → likely function. Use a real course micrograph to practise after you learn the pattern.

EPITHELIAL TISSUESimple or stratified?Squamous, cuboidal, or columnar?Four original schematics

01 / Read the structure

Two clues give you the name.

Epithelial tissue covers body surfaces, lines many internal passages and cavities, and forms glands. Its cells sit close together, with an exposed free surface on one side and a basement membrane on the other.

Most introductory identification begins with two questions: How many layers are there? and What shape are the cells at the free surface? The answers build the tissue name.

Classification rule: “Simple” means one cell layer; “stratified” means more than one. Squamous cells are flattened, cuboidal cells are roughly as tall as they are wide, and columnar cells are taller than they are wide.

02 / Four common patterns

Read the surface layer.

These are simplified schematics, not photomicrographs.
Real slides vary with stain and section angle.

01 / ONE LAYER · FLAT CELLS

Simple squamous

Thin cells favour rapid exchange or a smooth lining. Examples include lung alveoli and the lining of blood vessels.

02 / ONE LAYER · CUBE-LIKE CELLS

Simple cuboidal

Cube-like cells often absorb or secrete. Look for them in kidney tubules and many small gland ducts.

03 / ONE LAYER · TALL CELLS

Simple columnar

Tall cells commonly absorb and secrete. The digestive tract includes simple columnar epithelium, often with goblet cells.

04 / MANY LAYERS · FLAT SURFACE

Stratified squamous

Multiple layers protect against abrasion. It is keratinized in the epidermis and nonkeratinized in moist linings such as the mouth.

An epithelium is named by the cells at its free surface. A stratified tissue may have differently shaped cells deeper down.

03 / A repeatable lab method

Identify first. Interpret second.

Use structure as your evidence.
Location is a useful check, not a shortcut.

STEP 01

Count the layers.

Look for whether cells form one layer or several. A crowded section can make this tricky; follow the basement membrane.

STEP 02

Inspect the free edge.

Use the shape of the most exposed cells to choose squamous, cuboidal, or columnar.

STEP 03

Check special clues.

Look for cilia, goblet cells, keratin, or a dome-shaped surface. These can narrow the identification.

Common near-miss: pseudostratified ciliated columnar epithelium looks layered because nuclei sit at different heights, but each cell contacts the basement membrane. Transitional epithelium changes shape as the urinary tract stretches.

04 / Practise retrieval

Name it before you open the answer.

A single, very thin layer lines air sacs in the lungs. What pattern fits?

Simple squamous. It is one layer of flattened cells, which supports efficient gas exchange across a thin barrier.

A kidney tubule is lined by one layer of cells about as tall as they are wide.

Simple cuboidal. One layer gives “simple”; the roughly cube-shaped cells give “cuboidal.”

A digestive lining has one layer of tall cells, some with mucus-secreting goblet cells.

Simple columnar. The single layer and tall surface cells determine the name; goblet cells add a useful clue.

A protective surface has many layers and flattened cells at its exposed edge.

Stratified squamous. Name the tissue from the surface cells, not the deeper layers. Then check whether it is keratinized.

For stronger recall, cover the diagrams and explain each name aloud: layer count first, surface-cell shape second. Then compare your explanation with a labelled course slide.
